docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: Welcome to the Yuzuha API Reference. This section documents the types, functions, and modules of the yuzuha Python package, organized by role. The dependency runs in one direction — spins build edges, edges build specs, specs produce bases, and bases produce symbols.

docs.title: Core Types
docs.text:
The fundamental building blocks for specifying CG tensors:

Type Description Spin SU(2) irreducible representation label (half-integer \(j\)) Direction Arrow direction: incoming or outgoing Edge Directed representation — one external edge of a CG tensor CGSpec Full CG tensor specification: edges + internal fusion tree Contraction Edge-pair specification for X-symbol computation

docs.title: Symbols
docs.text:
The primary outputs of Yuzuha — recoupling coefficients as NumPy arrays:

Function Returns Description compute_xsymbol (ndarray, CGSpec) Recoupling coefficients for contracting two CG tensors; shape (om_a, om_b, om_c) compute_rsymbol (ndarray, CGSpec) Permutation transformation on the OM space; shape (om_in, om_out) canonical_basis ndarray Canonical CG basis tensor; shape (*external_dims, om_dim)

Two further functions handle duality, and are documented alongside the Metric Tensor:

Function Returns Description fs_phase_for_spin(spin) float Frobenius-Schur indicator \((-1)^{2j}\) compute_conjugate(spec) (float, CGSpec) Conjugate phase and arrow-reversed spec

docs.title: Primitives
docs.text:
The mathematical layer the symbols are built on. These live in Rust and are not callable from Python, but their conventions determine every value the library returns:

Topic Description Clebsch-Gordan Real CG coefficients in the Condon-Shortley convention Metric Tensor Arrow-reversal transformation \(g^{(j)}_{m,m'} = (-1)^{j-m}\delta_{m,-m'}\) Triangle Rules Triangle inequality and admissible spin range utilities

docs.text:
Caching is transparent, so these utilities are only needed when the cache's location or contents matter — in deployments, tests, or when inspecting what has accumulated:

docs.title: API Design Principles
docs.text:
Five commitments hold across the whole surface:

  • All outputs are NumPy arrays: Symbols are returned as float64 ndarray objects, compatible with standard scientific Python tools
  • Immutable specs: CGSpec objects are never mutated; with_inverted_axes returns a new object
  • Transparent caching: Cache lookups and stores are invisible to the caller; the same result is returned regardless of whether the cache was hit
  • Fail loudly: Invalid inputs (bad permutations, incompatible contractions, triangle violations) raise ValueError to avoid silently returning wrong results
  • Thread-safe caching: All database operations are protected by mutexes

docs.title: Cache Management
docs.text: Caching in Yuzuha is transparent — nothing on this page is needed to get correct results. These utilities exist for the cases where the cache's location or contents matter to you: pointing it at a writable directory in a deployment, inspecting how much has accumulated, and isolating it so that a test run neither reads nor pollutes real data.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Yuzuha maintains three persistent SQLite databases, each keyed on the inputs of the function whose results it holds:

Database File Content CG basis cache .yuzuha/cgbasis.db external spins → canonical basis array X-symbol cache .yuzuha/xsymbol.db (spec_a, spec_b, contraction) → (x_array, spec_c) R-symbol cache .yuzuha/rsymbol.db (spec, permutation) → (r_array, spec_permuted)

All three are created on first use and are thread-safe. The CG basis cache is managed by the Rust layer; the two symbol caches are managed by the Python layer, so the cache-clearing utilities below reach the latter two only.

docs.title: Cache Path
docs.text:
All three databases live in one directory, resolved in this priority order:

  1. Thread-local override, set by TestCacheContext — highest priority
  2. Environment variable YUZUHA_CACHE_PATH
  3. Default: .yuzuha/ in the current working directory

set_cache_path works by setting the environment variable, so it takes effect for the whole process but is still overridden inside a TestCacheContext block:

import yuzuha

# Set via Python
yuzuha.set_cache_path('/path/to/cache')

# Or via environment variable (before importing yuzuha)
# export YUZUHA_CACHE_PATH=/path/to/cache

docs.title: Inspecting Cache State
docs.text:
print_cache_stats is the quick human-readable view; get_cache_stats returns the same information as a dict of size, db_path, and db_size_bytes per cache, for logging or assertions:

import yuzuha

# Print a human-readable summary
yuzuha.print_cache_stats()
# X-symbol cache:
#   Entries: 42
#   Database: .yuzuha/xsymbol.db
#   Size: 1.2 MB
# R-symbol cache:
#   Entries: 18
#   Database: .yuzuha/rsymbol.db
#   Size: 0.5 MB

# Or get the raw dict
stats = yuzuha.get_cache_stats()
print(stats['xsymbol']['size'])        # number of cached X-symbols
print(stats['rsymbol']['db_path'])     # path to R-symbol database

docs.title: Isolated Cache for Testing
docs.text:
import yuzuha
from yuzuha import TestCacheContext

with TestCacheContext():
    # All cache operations use an isolated temporary directory
    x, spec_c = yuzuha.compute_xsymbol(spec_a, spec_b, contraction)
# Temporary cache is cleaned up automatically on exit

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: reset_caches() and clear_all_caches() do different things. The first closes and discards the in-memory cache objects so that the next symbol computation opens a fresh connection, leaving the stored data untouched. The second deletes the entries from the X- and R-symbol databases while preserving the files and their schema. Neither clears cgbasis.db; to discard cached canonical bases, delete that file.

docs.title: Database
docs.text: startup_database() pre-computes the canonical CG bases for the spin configurations a tensor network calculation is most likely to need, so that the cost is paid once at startup instead of as a cache miss in the middle of a run. It is purely an optimization: the cache fills itself on first use either way, and the results are identical.

docs.title: startup_database
docs.text:
startup_database(logger: Optional[Logger] = None, log_level: int = logging.INFO, special_spins: Optional[Sequence[int]] = None, general_spins: Optional[Sequence[int]] = None) -> None

Pre-compute and cache CG bases for commonly used spin configurations.

This function computes and caches: 1. 3rd order bases: one spin is 1/2 or 1, other two spins up to spin-3 2. 4th order bases: two spins are 1/2, other two spins up to spin-3

The database is automatically populated when bases are computed for the first time. Subsequent calls will use the cached values.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default logger Logger

Logger instance to use. If None, creates a default stream logger.

None log_level int

Logging level to use for the default logger. Default is logging.INFO.

INFO special_spins sequence of int

Doubled spin values for the distinguished edge of the 3rd order configurations. Defaults to (1, 2), i.e. j=1/2 and j=1.

None general_spins sequence of int

Doubled spin values for the remaining edges. Defaults to (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), i.e. j=1/2 through j=3.

None

Examples:

>>> import yuzuha
>>> yuzuha.startup_database()

>>> # With custom logger
>>> import logging
>>> logger = logging.getLogger('my_app')
>>> yuzuha.startup_database(logger=logger)

>>> # Narrow the sweep to j=1/2 and j=1 only
>>> yuzuha.startup_database(special_spins=[1], general_spins=[1, 2])

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The default sweep covers the configurations that dominate practical SU(2) tensor network work:

  • 3rd-order bases: one spin in \(\{1/2, 1\}\), the other two in \(\{1/2, 1, 3/2, 2, 5/2, 3\}\) — all 3! orderings of each triplet
  • 4th-order bases: two spins fixed at \(1/2\), two in \(\{1/2, 1, 3/2, 2, 5/2, 3\}\) — all \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) positions for the two fixed spins

Configurations already present in the database are not recomputed, so calling the function repeatedly is cheap and idempotent.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import yuzuha

# Basic usage — pre-populate with default logging
yuzuha.startup_database()

# With a custom logger
import logging
logger = logging.getLogger('my_app')
yuzuha.startup_database(logger=logger)

# Suppress output
yuzuha.startup_database(log_level=logging.WARNING)

# Narrow the sweep — doubled spin values, so 1 is j=1/2 and 2 is j=1
yuzuha.startup_database(special_spins=[1], general_spins=[1, 2])

special_spins is the grid for the distinguished edge of the 3rd-order configurations and general_spins the grid for the remaining edges, both as doubled values. Omitting them uses the default ranges above. Narrowing them is worthwhile when an application only ever sees a few spin values, or in tests where the full sweep would dominate the runtime.

docs.title: Progress Logging
docs.text:
Progress is logged at INFO level through the yuzuha.database logger, which reports:

  • the number of configurations to process
  • a running count, every 10 configurations
  • any configuration skipped for a triangle inequality violation
  • a final tally of successes and failures

Pass log_level=logging.WARNING to silence all of it, or logger= to route it into an application's own logging setup.

docs.title: Database Location
docs.text:
The canonical basis cache is written to cgbasis.db in the Yuzuha cache directory, resolved in the same priority order as the symbol caches:

  1. Thread-local test override, for test isolation
  2. YUZUHA_CACHE_PATH environment variable
  3. Default: .yuzuha/ in the current working directory

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Triangle inequality violations are not errors. A swept configuration for which no valid internal coupling exists is logged at DEBUG level, omitted from the success count, and skipped — so the number of entries created is smaller than the size of the grid swept.

docs.title: CGSpec
docs.text: CGSpec is the central data structure in Yuzuha: it identifies a CG tensor uniquely by recording its external edges together with the internal spins of its fusion tree. Every symbol function takes or returns one, and a spec doubles as the cache key under which the corresponding basis and symbol arrays are stored.

docs.title: CGSpec
docs.text:
Full specification of a CG tensor: external edges and the internal left-associative fusion tree.

Use from_edges to construct; do not call the constructor directly.

Examples:

>>> import yuzuha
>>> jhalf = yuzuha.Spin(1)
>>> spec  = yuzuha.CGSpec.from_edges([
...     yuzuha.Edge.incoming(jhalf),
...     yuzuha.Edge.incoming(jhalf),
...     yuzuha.Edge.outgoing(yuzuha.Spin(2)),
... ])
>>> print(spec.num_external())
3
>>> print(spec.om_dimension())
1

docs.title: with_inverted_axes
docs.text:
with_inverted_axes(axes: list[int]) -> CGSpec

Return a new CGSpec with the edge directions at the given axes flipped.

The internal OM configurations (alphas) are reused unchanged because they depend only on spin values, not directions.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default axes list[int]

Indices of edges whose direction should be flipped (Incoming ↔ Outgoing).

required

Returns:

Type Description CGSpec

A new CGSpec with the specified edge directions inverted.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If any axis index is out of bounds.

Examples:

>>> import yuzuha
>>> j = yuzuha.Spin(2)
>>> spec = yuzuha.CGSpec.from_edges([
...     yuzuha.Edge.incoming(j),
...     yuzuha.Edge.incoming(j),
...     yuzuha.Edge.outgoing(j),
... ])
>>> flipped = spec.with_inverted_axes([0, 1])
>>> [e.dir for e in flipped.edges]
[Direction.outgoing, Direction.outgoing, Direction.outgoing]

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A spec has two parts:

  • The external edges — a list of Edge values, one per external edge
  • The internal spins (\(\alpha\) values) — one per intermediate fusion step in the left-associative fusion tree

For an \(n\)th-order tensor there are \(n - 2\) internal spins. You never supply them by hand, and they are not exposed as a Python attribute: from_edges enumerates every internal spin configuration admitted by the triangle inequality and retains them internally, which makes the spec's outer multiplicity well defined. What you see of them is their count, through om_dimension().

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
import yuzuha

jhalf = yuzuha.Spin(1)   # j = 1/2
j1    = yuzuha.Spin(2)   # j = 1

# 3rd-order spec: two incoming spin-1/2, one outgoing spin-1
spec = yuzuha.CGSpec.from_edges([
    yuzuha.Edge.incoming(jhalf),
    yuzuha.Edge.incoming(jhalf),
    yuzuha.Edge.outgoing(j1),
])
print(spec.num_external())   # 3
print(spec.om_dimension())   # 1

# The external shape is derived from the edges
print(tuple(e.j.dimension() for e in spec.edges))   # (2, 2, 3)

docs.title: Key Properties
docs.text: Method / Attribute Description edges List of the external Edge values, in order num_external() Number of external edges om_dimension() Outer-multiplicity (OM) dimension — number of valid internal spin paths with_inverted_axes(axes) Returns a copy with selected edge directions flipped

docs.title: Axis Inversion
docs.text:
with_inverted_axes(axes) creates a new CGSpec with the edge directions at the given axis indices flipped (Incoming ↔ Outgoing). The internal spin configurations are preserved, because they depend only on the spin values and not on the arrows:

# Flip the direction of edge 0
spec_inv = spec.with_inverted_axes([0])

# Flip multiple edges
spec_inv2 = spec.with_inverted_axes([0, 2])

Tensor network algorithms use this when a contracted pair has to be re-expressed with its arrows reversed. The method supplies the flipped spec; the caller is responsible for the accompanying Frobenius-Schur phase \((-1)^{2j}\) per inverted bond, described under Metric Tensor.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
CGSpec objects are immutable and hashable, so they can be used as dictionary keys and in sets. with_inverted_axes always returns a new object; the original is unchanged.

from_edges raises ValueError if the edge list is too short (fewer than 2 edges) or if no valid internal spin configuration exists, which happens when the triangle inequality fails for every candidate path.

docs.title: Contraction
docs.text: A Contraction names the pairs of external edges to be joined when two CG tensors are contracted. It is the third argument of compute_xsymbol, and it is validated against both input specs: the paired edges must carry the same spin and opposite arrow directions, which makes the contraction a legal SU(2) pairing.

docs.title: Contraction
docs.text:
Contraction(axes_a: list[int], axes_b: list[int])

Edge-pair specification for contracting two CG tensors.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default axes_a list[int]

Edge indices from the first CGSpec to contract.

required axes_b list[int]

Edge indices from the second CGSpec to contract.

required

Examples:

>>> import yuzuha
>>> # Contract edge 2 of spec_a with edge 0 of spec_b
>>> c = yuzuha.Contraction([2], [0])
>>> # Contract two pairs simultaneously
>>> c2 = yuzuha.Contraction([2, 3], [0, 1])

docs.text:
axes_a: list[int]

Edge indices to contract from the first CGSpec.

Returns:

Type Description list[int]

Axis indices into spec A.

docs.title: axes_b property
docs.text:
axes_b: list[int]

Edge indices to contract from the second CGSpec.

Returns:

Type Description list[int]

Axis indices into spec B.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Each pair \((i, k)\) indicates that edge \(i\) of the first tensor (spec A) is contracted with edge \(k\) of the second tensor (spec B). The two index lists are given separately and matched up position by position:

import yuzuha

# Contract edge 2 of spec_a with edge 0 of spec_b
contraction = yuzuha.Contraction([2], [0])

# Contract multiple pairs
contractions = yuzuha.Contraction([2, 3], [0, 1])

docs.title: Fields
docs.text: Attribute Type Description axes_a list[int] Edge indices from spec A to contract axes_b list[int] Edge indices from spec B to contract

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
A Contraction is valid if:

  1. axes_a and axes_b have the same length
  2. Each index in axes_a is in range [0, spec_a.num_external())
  3. Each index in axes_b is in range [0, spec_b.num_external())
  4. For every pair \((i, k)\): the spin of edge \(i\) in spec A equals the spin of edge \(k\) in spec B
  5. For every pair \((i, k)\): the direction of edge \(i\) in spec A is opposite to the direction of edge \(k\) in spec B (one incoming, one outgoing)

Condition 1 is enforced by the constructor, since it needs nothing but the two lists. The remaining conditions depend on the specs being contracted and are therefore checked by compute_xsymbol, which raises ValueError on a violation.

docs.text:

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Contraction objects are immutable and hashable, support == comparison, and can be reused across any number of compute_xsymbol calls with compatible specs.

The order of the pairs matters. The pair at position 0 is treated as the first contraction, which feeds through to the edge order and hence the internal fusion tree of the output spec \(C\).

docs.title: Direction
docs.text: Direction is the two-valued enum recording whether an external edge is incoming (primal representation) or outgoing (dual representation). Arrow directions are not decoration: they decide how charges fuse, which magnetic-number sum has to vanish, and where the invariant metric must be inserted when an arrow is reversed.

Use the static constructors incoming() and outgoing() rather than instantiating directly.

Examples:

>>> import yuzuha
>>> d = yuzuha.Direction.incoming()
>>> print(d.sign())
1
>>> print(d.flip())

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Every external edge of a CG tensor carries one of the two directions, built with the static constructors or recovered from the dir field of an existing edge:

from yuzuha import Direction

d_in  = Direction.incoming()   # primal / ket-type index
d_out = Direction.outgoing()   # dual / bra-type index

print(d_in.sign())             # 1
print(d_out.sign())            # -1
print(d_in.flip() == d_out)    # True

docs.title: Sign Convention
docs.text:
An incoming edge contributes \(+m\) to the total magnetic quantum number and an outgoing edge contributes \(-m\). Charge conservation then requires the signed sum over all edges to vanish, and any basis entry whose indices violate this is identically zero:

\[\sum_{\text{incoming}} m_i - \sum_{\text{outgoing}} m_j = 0\]

The rule survives arrow reversal because its two moving parts cancel. Reversing an edge contracts it with the metric, which sends \(m \to -m\) on that edge, and at the same time flips the sign that edge carries in the sum. The law therefore holds in the same form for every arrow pattern, not merely the canonical one.

docs.title: Arrow Reversal
docs.text: Flipping a direction is not a relabeling — the tensor data has to be transformed with the invariant metric \(g\). Reversal from incoming to outgoing contracts with \(g\); reversal from outgoing to incoming contracts with \(g^{-1} = (-1)^{2j}\, g\), which is \(+g\) for integer spins and \(-g\) for half-integer spins. That sign is the Frobenius-Schur phase, which justifies Direction as part of the cache key of every symbol.

docs.title: Edge
docs.text: An Edge is a Spin paired with a Direction, describing one external edge of a CG tensor. Edges are the unit a CGSpec is assembled from: the ordered list of edges fixes both the external shape of every tensor built from the spec and the fusion order of its internal tree.

The two class-method constructors are the primary way to create edges, and take a Spin object from a doubled integer:

import yuzuha

j = yuzuha.Spin(1)   # j = 1/2

e_in  = yuzuha.Edge.incoming(j)   # spin-1/2 incoming edge
e_out = yuzuha.Edge.outgoing(j)   # spin-1/2 outgoing edge

print(e_in.j)              # 1/2
print(e_in.is_incoming())  # True

The direction can also be tested with is_incoming() and is_outgoing(), which avoids having to compare against a Direction value. The edge's dimension is not stored separately: it is j.dimension(), the number \(2j + 1\) of magnetic quantum number states, and it becomes one axis of the canonical basis array.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Edge objects are immutable and hashable, so they can be used as dictionary keys and in sets. Two edges are equal only when both their spin and their direction agree.

Flipping an arrow — turning an incoming edge into an outgoing edge of the same spin, or the reverse — is not just a matter of swapping the direction field. The tensor data must also be contracted with the invariant metric; see Metric Tensor.

docs.title: Spin
docs.text: Spin labels an SU(2) irreducible representation by its spin quantum number \(j \in \{0, \tfrac{1}{2}, 1, \tfrac{3}{2}, \ldots\}\). It is the atom the other core types are built from: an Edge pairs a Spin with a direction, a CGSpec is built from edges, and the dimension \(2j + 1\) a Spin reports fixes the shape of every basis and symbol array derived from it.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Spins are stored internally as the doubled integer \(2j\), so that no part of the library performs floating-point arithmetic on a representation label. Comparisons, triangle-rule checks, and cache keys are therefore all exact integer operations. The price is that the constructor takes the doubled value in place of \(j\) itself:

import yuzuha

j0    = yuzuha.Spin(0)   # j = 0
jhalf = yuzuha.Spin(1)   # j = 1/2
j1    = yuzuha.Spin(2)   # j = 1
j32   = yuzuha.Spin(3)   # j = 3/2

value() converts back to a Python float where a human-readable \(j\) is wanted, and twice() exposes the stored integer for code that needs to key on it. is_integer() and is_half_integer() partition the spins by Frobenius-Schur class, which decides the sign picked up on arrow reversal — see Metric Tensor.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Spin values are immutable. Equality, hashing, and < ordering are all supported: Spin objects can be used as dictionary keys and in sets, and lists of spins can be passed to sorted() directly without a key function. The ordering is on the doubled integer, which supplies the total order the protocol requires of a representation label.

The identity representation is Spin(0) (\(j = 0\)), which has dimension 1 and contributes a trivial factor in all coupling coefficients. A negative doubled value raises ValueError.

docs.title: Clebsch-Gordan Coefficients
docs.text: Clebsch-Gordan coefficients are the lowest layer Yuzuha builds on: every canonical basis is a contraction of them along a fusion tree, and every symbol is a projection onto such bases. They are computed in the Rust layer and are not exposed as a Python function, so this page documents the convention and properties.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A CG coefficient gives the decomposition of the tensor product of two SU(2) representations into irreducible components:

\[C^{j_3 m_3}_{j_1 m_1,\, j_2 m_2} \equiv \langle j_1 m_1,\, j_2 m_2 \mid j_3 m_3 \rangle\]

Yuzuha uses the Condon-Shortley convention, which fixes the relative phases so that every coefficient is real-valued. That choice allows all of Yuzuha's outputs to be float64 arrays without complex involvement.

docs.title: Selection Rules
docs.text:
A coefficient whose indices violate any of the following is identically zero, so these rules also determine which internal spin paths a CGSpec admits at all:

Rule Condition Magnetic conservation \(m_1 + m_2 = m_3\) Triangle inequality \(\lvert j_1 - j_2 \rvert \leq j_3 \leq j_1 + j_2\) Integer sum \(j_1 + j_2 + j_3 \in \mathbb{Z}\) Range \(-j_i \leq m_i \leq j_i\) for each \(i\)

docs.title: Orthonormality Relations
docs.text:
The coefficients form an orthonormal basis in both directions. Summing over the uncoupled magnetic numbers gives column orthonormality:

\[\sum_{m_1, m_2} C^{j_3 m_3}_{j_1 m_1, j_2 m_2}\, C^{j_3' m_3'}_{j_1 m_1, j_2 m_2} = \delta_{j_3 j_3'}\, \delta_{m_3 m_3'}\]

Summing over the coupled ones gives row orthonormality:

\[\sum_{j_3, m_3} C^{j_3 m_3}_{j_1 m_1, j_2 m_2}\, C^{j_3 m_3}_{j_1 m_1', j_2 m_2'} = \delta_{m_1 m_1'}\, \delta_{m_2 m_2'}\]

The first relation is what propagates to the orthonormality of the canonical basis once the coefficients are contracted along a fusion tree.

docs.title: Internal Access
docs.text: The Rust layer provides clebsch_gordan(j1, m1, j2, m2, j3, m3), called by canonical_basis as it walks the fusion tree. There is no Python binding: individual coefficients are an implementation detail, and exposing them would invite callers to rebuild bases by hand under a different normalization.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text: Coefficients are cached in-process by the Rust layer (once_cell), keyed on the full index tuple \((j_1, m_1, j_2, m_2, j_3, m_3)\). Individual values are never written to disk; what persists on disk is the assembled canonical basis tensor, which is the unit of reuse that matters in practice.

docs.text: The implementation evaluates the standard Racah formula, an explicit algebraic sum over factorials of the angular momentum quantum numbers, and caches the result. Large spins are not a performance concern in practice: the cost is paid once per index tuple and the cached canonical bases absorb the rest.

docs.title: Metric Tensor
docs.text: The invariant metric makes arrow directions tractable: it is the transformation that turns an index in a representation space into an index in its dual. Yuzuha applies it automatically wherever a spec's arrows deviate from the canonical pattern, and the sign it carries for half-integer spins is the Frobenius-Schur phase that surfaces in every arrow-reversal and bond-inversion rule in the library.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The invariant metric \(g^{(j)}\) implements the canonical isomorphism between a representation and its dual:

\[g^{(j)}_{m,\,m'} = (-1)^{j - m}\,\delta_{m,\,-m'}\]

This is a \((2j+1) \times (2j+1)\) real orthogonal matrix. Its defining properties are

\[g^{(j)} \cdot \left(g^{(j)}\right)^\top = I, \qquad \left(g^{(j)}\right)^2 = (-1)^{2j}\, I,\]

so the metric is symmetric (\(g^\top = g\)) for integer spins and antisymmetric (\(g^\top = -g\)) for half-integer ones, which can be written uniformly as \(g^\top = (-1)^{2j} g\).

docs.title: Arrow Reversal
docs.text:
To convert an incoming edge to an outgoing one, contract with \(g\):

\[\tilde{T}^{m'}_{\ldots} = \sum_m g^{(j)}_{m, m'}\, T^{\ldots}_{m}\]

To go the other way, contract with the inverse:

\[\tilde{T}_{\ldots m'} = \sum_m \left(g^{(j)}\right)^{-1}_{m', m}\, T^{\ldots m}\]

The two directions are not interchangeable. Because \(g^{-1} = (-1)^{2j}\, g^\top\), they differ by a sign for half-integer spins, and this is exactly the asymmetry a tensor network algorithm has to account for when it reverses a bond.

docs.title: Frobenius-Schur Indicator
docs.text:
That recurring sign is the Frobenius-Schur indicator:

\[\text{FS}(j) = (-1)^{2j} = \begin{cases} +1 & j \in \mathbb{Z} \\ -1 & j \in \mathbb{Z} + \tfrac{1}{2} \end{cases}\]

It is \(+1\) for integer representations and \(-1\) for half-integer ones. In the X-symbol bond inversion scheme, flipping a contracted pair of spin \(j\) multiplies the X-symbol by \(\text{FS}(j)\); the same factor accumulates once per deviating edge in the conjugate phase.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
The metric itself is a Rust-level primitive (use_as_incoming, use_as_outgoing in yuzuha::primitives) and is applied for you inside canonical_basis. What the Python namespace exposes are the two derived quantities a caller actually needs:

Function Returns Description fs_phase_for_spin(spin) float Frobenius-Schur indicator \((-1)^{2j}\) compute_conjugate(spec) (float, CGSpec) Conjugate phase and the arrow-reversed spec 
import yuzuha

jhalf = yuzuha.Spin(1)   # j = 1/2
j1    = yuzuha.Spin(2)   # j = 1

# Frobenius-Schur phase
phase_half = yuzuha.fs_phase_for_spin(jhalf)   # -1.0  (half-integer)
phase_int  = yuzuha.fs_phase_for_spin(j1)      # +1.0  (integer)

# Conjugation returns the accumulated phase alongside the reversed spec
spec = yuzuha.CGSpec.from_edges([
    yuzuha.Edge.incoming(jhalf),
    yuzuha.Edge.incoming(jhalf),
    yuzuha.Edge.outgoing(j1),
])
conj_phase, conj_spec = yuzuha.compute_conjugate(spec)

docs.text: The metric \(g^{(j)}\) is not the Euclidean metric. It is the unique SU(2)-invariant bilinear form on \(V_j\) up to a global phase, and substituting the identity matrix for it produces arrow-reversal results that are silently incorrect, though the shapes still match.

docs.title: Triangle Rules
docs.text: The triangle rules decide which spin triplets can couple at all, and so they decide the shape of everything downstream: they allow CGSpec.from_edges to enumerate internal spin paths, they fix a spec's outer-multiplicity dimension, and they are what a Contraction is validated against. Like the CG coefficients, they live in the Rust layer and have no Python binding.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Three spins satisfy the triangle inequality if and only if they can be the sides of a triangle in the usual sense, with the extra requirement that their sum be an integer:

\[|j_1 - j_2| \leq j_3 \leq j_1 + j_2 \quad \text{and} \quad j_1 + j_2 + j_3 \in \mathbb{Z}\]

For a fixed pair \(j_1, j_2\), the admissible coupled spins therefore form a contiguous ladder in unit steps,

\[j_3 \in \{|j_1 - j_2|,\; |j_1 - j_2| + 1,\; \ldots,\; j_1 + j_2\},\]

whose length is \(N = j_1 + j_2 - |j_1 - j_2| + 1 = 2\min(j_1, j_2) + 1\). That count is the branching factor at one node of a fusion tree, and the product of such factors over the tree bounds the outer multiplicity of a spec.

docs.title: Enumeration in CGSpec Construction
docs.text:
CGSpec.from_edges walks the left-associative fusion tree, applying the ladder above at each step and discarding paths that dead-end:

  1. The first internal spin \(\alpha_1\) ranges over the admissible spins of \((j_1, j_2)\)
  2. Each subsequent \(\alpha_k\) ranges over the admissible spins of \((\alpha_{k-1}, j_{k+1})\)
  3. The last coupling must land exactly on the terminal edge's spin \(j_n\)

Step 3 is why a spec can have an OM dimension smaller than the naive product of branching factors, and why an edge list can be rejected outright: if no path survives, from_edges raises ValueError.

docs.title: Canonical Basis
docs.text: The canonical basis is the explicit CG tensor a CGSpec stands for, written out in the magnetic-quantum-number basis. It is the object from which both symbols are derived — X-symbols by contracting and projecting a pair of bases, R-symbols by overlapping a basis with its permuted counterpart — so most users reach for it only when they need the raw coupling tensor itself.

docs.title: canonical_basis builtin
docs.text:
canonical_basis(spec: CGSpec) -> NDArray[np.float64]

Compute canonical basis data for a coupled gauge tree.

Computes the transformation matrix from magnetic quantum number basis to outer multiplicity (OM) basis for a given CGSpec. The basis is cached for efficiency using an SQLite database.

The canonical basis is only defined for CGSpecs with at least 2 external edges.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default spec CGSpec

The CGSpec for which to compute the canonical basis.

required

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

The canonical basis transformation matrix. Shape depends on the CGSpec: - For n external edges with spins j_i, shape is [d_1, d_2, ..., d_n, om_dim] where d_i = 2*j_i + 1 is the dimension of the i-th edge, and om_dim is the outer multiplicity dimension.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the CGSpec has fewer than 2 external edges.

RuntimeError

If computation fails or cache error occurs.

Examples:

>>> import yuzuha
>>> j_half = yuzuha.Spin(1)  # j=1/2
>>> spec = yuzuha.CGSpec.from_edges([
...     yuzuha.Edge.incoming(j_half),
...     yuzuha.Edge.incoming(j_half),
...     yuzuha.Edge.incoming(j_half)
... ])
>>> basis = yuzuha.canonical_basis(spec)
>>> print(basis.shape)

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
canonical_basis(spec) returns a real-valued NumPy array of shape (*external_dims, om_dim), where:

  • external_dims is the tuple \((2j_0+1, \ldots, 2j_{n-1}+1)\) — one factor per external edge, equal to its representation dimension
  • om_dim is spec.om_dimension() — the number of valid internal spin paths

Each slice basis[..., mu] is the CG tensor for OM index \(\mu\), built by contracting Clebsch-Gordan coefficients along the left-associative fusion tree described in Core Concepts. Edges whose direction deviates from the canonical pattern are corrected by contracting with the invariant metric, so the array returned is always the basis for the spec as given.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import yuzuha
import numpy as np

jhalf = yuzuha.Spin(1)   # j = 1/2
j1    = yuzuha.Spin(2)   # j = 1

spec = yuzuha.CGSpec.from_edges([
    yuzuha.Edge.incoming(jhalf),
    yuzuha.Edge.incoming(jhalf),
    yuzuha.Edge.outgoing(j1),
])

basis = yuzuha.canonical_basis(spec)
print(basis.shape)    # (2, 2, 3, 1) — (d_j1, d_j2, d_j3, om_dim)
print(basis.dtype)    # float64

# Every OM slice is a unit vector over the magnetic indices
print(np.linalg.norm(basis[..., 0]))   # 1.0

docs.title: Normalization Convention
docs.text:
The slices form an orthonormal set with respect to the inner product that sums over all magnetic quantum number indices:

\[\langle B_\mu | B_ u angle = \sum_{m_0, \ldots, m_{n-1}} B_\mu(m_0, \ldots, m_{n-1})\, B_ u(m_0, \ldots, m_{n-1}) = \delta_{\mu u}\]

This is not the normalization of the bare Clebsch-Gordan coefficients. For a 3rd-order tensor, where the OM dimension is always 1, the single basis element carries a factor of \(1/\sqrt{2j_3 + 1}\) relative to the bare coefficient:

\[B_0(m_1, m_2, m_3) = rac{1}{\sqrt{2j_3 + 1}}\, C^{j_3 m_3}_{j_1 m_1,\, j_2 m_2}\]

docs.title: Caching
docs.text: Canonical bases are cached by the Rust layer in .yuzuha/cgbasis.db, keyed on the external spins alone — arrow directions are stripped, since a deviating spec is derived from the stored tensor by applying the metric. The cache is populated on first use and persists across Python sessions; startup_database() pre-computes it for the spin configurations most commonly needed, trading startup time for predictable latency later.

docs.title: R-Symbol
docs.text: The R-symbol is the transformation a CG tensor's outer-multiplicity index undergoes when its external edges are permuted. Permuting the axes of a symmetry-constrained tensor is not a pure reindexing — the fusion tree is rebuilt in a different order — and the R-symbol is the matrix that carries the reduced blocks from the old OM basis to the new one.

docs.title: compute_rsymbol
docs.text:
compute_rsymbol(spec, permutation) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, CGSpec]

Compute R-symbol for tensor edge permutation with caching.

The R-symbol represents how outer multiplicity indices transform under permutation of tensor edges. Results are cached to avoid redundant computations.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default spec CGSpec

The CGSpec to permute.

required permutation list[int]

Permutation of external edge indices. Must be a valid permutation (each index from 0 to num_external-1 appears exactly once).

required

Returns:

Type Description tuple[ndarray, CGSpec]

A tuple containing: - R-symbol array of shape [om_original, om_permuted]. - Permuted CGSpec with edges reordered according to permutation.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the permutation is invalid.

RuntimeError

If computation fails.

Examples:

>>> import yuzuha
>>> j_half = yuzuha.Spin(1)
>>> spec = yuzuha.CGSpec.from_edges([
...     yuzuha.Edge.incoming(j_half),
...     yuzuha.Edge.incoming(j_half),
...     yuzuha.Edge.incoming(j_half),
...     yuzuha.Edge.incoming(j_half)
... ])
>>> # Swap first two edges
>>> permutation = [1, 0, 2, 3]
>>> r_array, spec_permuted = yuzuha.compute_rsymbol(spec, permutation)
>>> print(r_array.shape)

Notes

The first call for a given set of parameters will compute the result and cache it. Subsequent calls with the same parameters will return the cached result, which is typically much faster.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The R-symbol \(R^{\mu'}_{\mu}\) is the overlap between the permuted and the original canonical basis:

\[R^{\mu'}_{\mu} = \langle \text{permuted},{\mu'} | \text{original},\mu \rangle\]

The returned array has shape (om_original, om_permuted). For OM dimension 1 it degenerates to a \(1 \times 1\) matrix holding the permutation phase \(\pm 1\); for higher OM dimensions it is a genuine orthogonal rotation of the multiplicity space.

docs.title: Permutation Convention
docs.text: The permutation is given as a list of source indices: permutation[i] is the position in the original spec whose edge moves to position i of the permuted spec, so that spec_permuted.edges[i] == spec.edges[permutation[i]]. This is the same convention NumPy's transpose uses, which makes the two safe to apply in tandem to a tensor and its reduced blocks.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import yuzuha
import numpy as np

jhalf = yuzuha.Spin(1)   # j = 1/2

spec = yuzuha.CGSpec.from_edges([
    yuzuha.Edge.incoming(jhalf),
    yuzuha.Edge.incoming(jhalf),
    yuzuha.Edge.incoming(jhalf),
    yuzuha.Edge.outgoing(yuzuha.Spin(3)),  # j = 3/2
])

# Swap the first two edges
r_array, spec_permuted = yuzuha.compute_rsymbol(spec, [1, 0, 2, 3])

print(r_array.shape)   # (om_original, om_permuted)
print(r_array.dtype)   # float64

# The identity permutation gives the identity matrix
r_id, _ = yuzuha.compute_rsymbol(spec, [0, 1, 2, 3])
assert np.allclose(r_id, np.eye(spec.om_dimension()))

docs.title: Algebraic Properties
docs.text:
The R-symbol is always unitary, and since it is real this amounts to orthogonality:

\[R^\top R = R R^\top = I\]

R-symbols also compose under composition of permutations, and the inverse permutation gives the transpose:

\[R(\sigma \circ \pi) = R(\sigma)\, R(\pi), \qquad R(\pi^{-1}) = R(\pi)^\top\]

Together these make a sequence of axis permutations collapsible into a single matrix, which is the practical reason for caching R-symbols to avoid recomputing them per permutation step:

r, _ = yuzuha.compute_rsymbol(spec, [1, 0, 2, 3])
assert np.allclose(r.T @ r, np.eye(r.shape[1]))

docs.title: Caching
docs.text: The first call for a given (spec, permutation) pair stores the result in .yuzuha/rsymbol.db. Subsequent calls return the cached value immediately.

An invalid permutation raises ValueError: wrong length, an out-of-range index, or a repeated index.

docs.title: X-Symbol
docs.text: The X-symbol is the recoupling coefficient for contracting two CG tensors: it says how the outer-multiplicity indices of the two inputs combine into the outer-multiplicity index of the result. It is the symbol a tensor network contraction actually needs, since contracting the symmetry-constrained parts of two tensors reduces to a dense contraction of their reduced blocks followed by multiplication with this coefficient.

docs.title: compute_xsymbol
docs.text:
compute_xsymbol(spec_a, spec_b, contraction) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, CGSpec]

Given two CGTs A and B with a contraction specification, computes the X-symbol tensor X^γ_{αβ} representing the coupling to output CGT C. Results are cached to avoid redundant computations.

The X-symbol is computed by: 1. Building canonical basis tensors for A and B 2. Contracting them over the specified edges (keeping OM indices separate) 3. Projecting the result onto the canonical basis of C

Name Type Description Default spec_a CGSpec

required spec_b CGSpec

Second CG specification

required contraction Contraction

Specification of which edges to contract

required

A tuple containing: - X-symbol array of shape [om_a, om_b, om_c] - Output CGSpec with edges from uncontracted A and B edges

Raises:

>>> import yuzuha
>>> j_half = yuzuha.Spin(1)
>>> j1 = yuzuha.Spin(2)
>>> spec_a = yuzuha.CGSpec.from_edges([
...     yuzuha.Edge.incoming(j_half),

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The X-symbol \(X^{\gamma}_{\alpha\beta}\) is a 3-index real tensor giving the expansion of the contracted product of the input bases in terms of the output basis:

\[A_\alpha \otimes_{\text{contracted}} B_\beta = \sum_\gamma X^\gamma_{\alpha\beta}\, C_\gamma, \qquad X^{\gamma}_{\alpha\beta} = \langle C_\gamma \mid A_\alpha \otimes_{\text{contracted}} B_\beta \rangle\]

The indices \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\) run over the OM spaces of specs A, B, and C, so the returned array has shape (om_a, om_b, om_c). In general \(\mathrm{om}_A \cdot \mathrm{om}_B \neq \mathrm{om}_C\), which means \(\mathbf{X}\) is a rectangular tensor with no unitarity or orthonormality property to rely on — unlike the R-symbol.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import yuzuha

jhalf = yuzuha.Spin(1)   # j = 1/2
j1    = yuzuha.Spin(2)   # j = 1

spec_a = yuzuha.CGSpec.from_edges([
    yuzuha.Edge.incoming(jhalf),
    yuzuha.Edge.incoming(jhalf),
    yuzuha.Edge.outgoing(j1),
])
spec_b = yuzuha.CGSpec.from_edges([
    yuzuha.Edge.incoming(j1),
    yuzuha.Edge.outgoing(jhalf),
    yuzuha.Edge.outgoing(jhalf),
])

# Contract edge 2 of spec_a (outgoing j=1) with edge 0 of spec_b (incoming j=1)
contraction = yuzuha.Contraction([2], [0])

x_array, spec_c = yuzuha.compute_xsymbol(spec_a, spec_b, contraction)
print(x_array.shape)         # (1, 1, 2) — (om_a, om_b, om_c)
print(x_array.dtype)         # float64
print(spec_c.num_external()) # 4 — uncontracted edges from A and B

docs.title: Output Spec
docs.text: The returned spec_c describes the output CG tensor. Its edges are the uncontracted edges of spec A followed by the uncontracted edges of spec B, each group keeping the relative order it had in its original spec. Its internal fusion tree then follows from the left-associative convention applied to that concatenated edge list, so the order of the pairs in the Contraction is significant.

docs.title: Computation Procedure
docs.text:
The projection onto spec C distinguishes the X-symbol from a plain tensor contraction, and it requires a third basis to be built:

  1. Compute the canonical bases for specs A and B, of shapes (*dims_a, om_a) and (*dims_b, om_b)
  2. Contract the two basis tensors over the magnetic-quantum-number axes named by the contraction, keeping the OM axes separate
  3. Build the canonical basis for the output spec C, of shape (*dims_c, om_c)
  4. Project the contracted result onto that basis to extract \(X^{\gamma}_{\alpha\beta}\)

docs.title: Caching
docs.text: The first call for a given (spec_a, spec_b, contraction) triple computes the result from scratch via Rust and stores it in .yuzuha/xsymbol.db. Subsequent calls with the same arguments return the cached result immediately.

docs.text:

docs.text:
If you find a bug or have a feature request, please open an issue on GitHub. Recoupling coefficients are easy to disagree about for convention reasons, so a report is far more useful with the following, which separates a convention mismatch from a genuine bug:

  • Your Python and NumPy versions
  • A minimal reproducible example, including how the CGSpec was constructed
  • The expected and actual output, and where the expectation comes from if it is a published table or another library

docs.title: Submitting Pull Requests
docs.text:
The usual GitHub flow applies:

  1. Fork the repository on GitHub
  2. Create a branch for your change
  3. Make your changes, adding tests where appropriate
  4. Run the test suite and ensure it passes
  5. Open a pull request with a clear description of your changes

Changes that alter computed values deserve particular care, because cached results from an earlier version remain on disk and will be returned in preference to the new computation. If a change is intended to alter outputs, say so in the pull request description so that the cache-invalidation question gets addressed.

docs.title: Development Setup
docs.text:
Building from source requires Rust 1.85 or higher; the installation guide covers the toolchain setup. Note that maturin develop compiles the extension into the active environment, so the build step has to be repeated after every change to the Rust sources — editable installs only cover the Python layer.

git clone https://github.com/Ideogenesis-AI/Yuzuha.git
cd Yuzuha

# Install dev dependencies
pip install -e ".[dev]"

# Build the Rust extension
maturin develop --release

# Run tests
pytest

docs.title: Running Tests
docs.text:
Yuzuha has two test suites:

# Python tests (pytest)
pytest

# Rust tests (cargo). The integration suite needs the test-utils feature,
# which exposes TestCacheGuard for cache isolation.
cargo test --features test-utils

The Python suite covers the full API including integration tests. The Rust suite covers internal algorithms like CG coefficient computation and CGSpec logic.

docs.title: Where to Place a Rust Test
docs.text:
Rust tests live in two places, and which one you pick is determined by what the test asserts, not by what it happens to call.

Inline #[cfg(test)] mod tests, at the bottom of the source file, holds unit tests of a single function: constructors, accessors, Display and operator impls, and error branches. Anything that touches a private item must go here, because tests/rust/ can only reach the public API. get_db_path, init_db, serialize_spins and reset_connection in src/builders/cache.rs, and build_permuted_spec in src/builders/rsymbol.rs, are only testable from inline modules.

tests/rust/ holds tests of mathematical properties that span several functions: orthonormality of the canonical basis, unitarity of R-symbols, F-symbol and X-symbol consistency between equivalent contraction paths, Clebsch-Gordan values checked against published tables, and concurrency behaviour. These tests exercise the crate the way a downstream user would, through yuzuha:: imports only.

Shared fixtures for the integration suite belong in tests/rust/common.rs. New integration files must be registered in tests/rust.rs, which is the single entry point Cargo compiles.

docs.title: Test Coverage
docs.text:
The project holds production line coverage above 95% for the Rust library, the Python bindings, and the Python package independently. Production coverage excludes lines inside inline #[cfg(test)] modules, so a file cannot raise its score by testing its own test code.

# One-off tooling setup; Coverage.py comes with the dev extras
cargo install cargo-llvm-cov
rustup component add llvm-tools-preview

# Rust library
cargo llvm-cov --features test-utils --summary-only

# Python package
coverage run --source yuzuha -m pytest && coverage report -m

Install llvm-tools-preview without relying on a system LLVM: the coverage format is versioned with the compiler, and an llvm-cov from Xcode or Homebrew will refuse to read profiles produced by rustc.

Two caveats when reading those numbers. cargo llvm-cov counts inline test modules, which are themselves almost fully covered, so its figure is optimistic relative to the metric above; use --lcov output and discard the lines at or after each file's first #[cfg(test)] to reproduce the production figure. And src/bindings.rs is absent from the report entirely, because it only compiles under the python feature — measuring it means building an extension with RUSTFLAGS="-C instrument-coverage", running pytest against that build with LLVM_PROFILE_FILE set, and reporting the resulting profiles with llvm-cov. Remember to reinstall a clean release build afterwards, since an instrumented extension is slow and writes profile data on every run.

When adding code, check the uncovered lines instead of the percentage. A few lines are genuinely unreachable and are expected to stay uncovered: the ? arms on the infallible build_cg3 in src/builders/builders.rs, and the InvalidMagneticNumber, TriangleViolation and InvalidContraction conversion arms in src/bindings.rs, which nothing in the crate ever constructs on a path reachable from Python.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: Before using Yuzuha, it helps to understand the mathematical objects and conventions the library is built around. This page introduces spins, edges, CG specifications, fusion trees, the outer-multiplicity index, and the caching model.

docs.title: Spin Representations
docs.text:
In SU(2) theory, every irreducible representation is labeled by a non-negative half-integer spin \(j \in \{0, \frac{1}{2}, 1, \frac{3}{2}, \ldots\}\). The dimension of the representation is \(2j + 1\).

Yuzuha represents spins internally as doubled integer values to avoid floating-point arithmetic. Spin(n) corresponds to \(j = n/2\):

import yuzuha

j0   = yuzuha.Spin(0)   # j = 0   (singlet)
jhalf = yuzuha.Spin(1)  # j = 1/2 (doublet)
j1   = yuzuha.Spin(2)   # j = 1   (triplet)
j32  = yuzuha.Spin(3)   # j = 3/2 (quartet)

print(jhalf.value())      # 0.5
print(jhalf.dimension())  # 2  (= 2j+1)
print(jhalf.twice())      # 1  (the internal integer 2j)

docs.title: Arrow Directions
docs.text:
Tensor network edges carry a direction — incoming or outgoing — that determines whether the edge transforms in the primal or dual representation. Arrow direction is crucial for computing the correct coupling coefficients and for arrow-reversal transformations via the invariant metric.

from yuzuha import Direction

d_in  = Direction.incoming()   # primal representation
d_out = Direction.outgoing()   # dual representation

Arrow directions can be flipped using the invariant metric \(g\):

\[g^{(j)}_{m,m'} = (-1)^{j-m}\,\delta_{m,-m'}\]

See Metric Tensor for the functions that implement this transformation.

docs.title: Edges
docs.text:
An Edge pairs a spin with a direction, representing one external edge of a tensor. The two constructors below are the usual way to build one, and the pair is readable afterwards through the j and dir fields:

import yuzuha

j = yuzuha.Spin(1)  # j = 1/2

e_in  = yuzuha.Edge.incoming(j)   # spin-1/2 incoming edge
e_out = yuzuha.Edge.outgoing(j)   # spin-1/2 outgoing edge

print(e_in.j, e_in.is_incoming())   # 1/2 True

docs.title: CG Specifications
docs.text:
A CGSpec (Clebsch-Gordan specification) fully describes a CG tensor — the canonical basis element of a tensor network node. It records:

  • The list of edges (spin + direction for each external edge)
  • The list of internal spins (\(\alpha\) values) — one per intermediate fusion step

For an \(n\)th-order tensor there are \(n - 2\) internal spins, determined by the left-associative fusion tree structure (see below).

import yuzuha

jhalf = yuzuha.Spin(1)  # j = 1/2
j1    = yuzuha.Spin(2)  # j = 1

# 3rd-order spec: two spin-1/2 incoming, one spin-1 outgoing
spec = yuzuha.CGSpec.from_edges([
    yuzuha.Edge.incoming(jhalf),
    yuzuha.Edge.incoming(jhalf),
    yuzuha.Edge.outgoing(j1),
])

print(spec.num_external())  # 3
print(spec.om_dimension())  # 1  (only one valid internal coupling)

# The external shape is read off the edges
print(tuple(e.j.dimension() for e in spec.edges))   # (2, 2, 3)

The from_edges constructor automatically enumerates all valid internal spin configurations. They are kept internally rather than exposed as an attribute; what you observe of them is their count, through om_dimension().

docs.title: Left-Associative Fusion Trees
docs.text:
Yuzuha represents multi-spin couplings using left-associative fusion trees. For \(n\) external spins \((j_1, j_2, \ldots, j_n)\), the coupling proceeds from left to right:

\[\bigl(\cdots\bigl((j_1 \otimes j_2) \otimes j_3\bigr) \otimes \cdots\bigr) \otimes j_n\]

Each step produces an intermediate spin \(\alpha_k\). For \(n\) edges there are \(n - 2\) intermediate spins \(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_{n-2}\):

  • 3 edges: \(j_1 \otimes j_2 \to \alpha_1 = j_3\) — no free internal spin
  • 4 edges: \((j_1 \otimes j_2 \to \alpha_1) \otimes j_3 \to j_4\) — one free internal spin

docs.title: Outer Multiplicity (OM) Index
docs.text:
When the same total spin \(j\) can be reached via multiple internal spin paths \((\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_{n-2})\), those paths are distinguished by the outer multiplicity (OM) index \(\mu\). The OM dimension is the number of such valid paths.

The OM index appears as the last axis of canonical basis tensors and as axes of X-symbol and R-symbol matrices.

# 4th-order spec with non-trivial OM
j1    = yuzuha.Spin(2)   # j = 1
jhalf = yuzuha.Spin(1)   # j = 1/2

spec = yuzuha.CGSpec.from_edges([
    yuzuha.Edge.incoming(j1),
    yuzuha.Edge.incoming(j1),
    yuzuha.Edge.incoming(j1),
    yuzuha.Edge.outgoing(j1),
])
print(spec.om_dimension())  # 3 — three internal spins couple j=1 x j=1 down to j=1

Four edges is the smallest order at which this can happen, and even then only if the spins permit more than one path. A 3rd-order spec always has OM dimension 1, because its single coupling is already fixed by the outgoing edge.

docs.title: Canonical CG Bases
docs.text:
The canonical basis for a CGSpec is a real-valued tensor of shape \((2j_1+1, \ldots, 2j_n+1, \mathrm{om\_dim})\) that expresses the CG tensor in the magnetic-quantum-number basis. It is computed from the CG coefficients along the left-associative fusion tree, then normalized so that the OM slices are orthonormal — each slice is a unit vector over the magnetic indices, which is not the normalization of the bare CG coefficients themselves.

basis = yuzuha.canonical_basis(spec)
print(basis.shape)  # (*external_dims, om_dim)

The canonical basis is the fundamental object from which X-symbols and R-symbols are derived.

docs.title: X-Symbols and R-Symbols
docs.text:
X-symbols are the recoupling coefficients for contracting two CG tensors:

\[X^{\gamma}_{\alpha\beta} = \langle C_\gamma | A_\alpha \otimes_{\text{contracted}} B_\beta \rangle\]

They form a 3-index tensor of shape \((\mathrm{om}_A, \mathrm{om}_B, \mathrm{om}_C)\).

R-symbols are the transformation matrices for permuting edges of a CG tensor:

\[R^{\mu'}_{\mu} = \langle \text{permuted},{\mu'} | \text{original},\mu \rangle\]

They form a 2-index unitary matrix of shape (om_original, om_permuted).

See X-Symbol and R-Symbol for the full API.

docs.title: SQLite Caching
docs.text:
Yuzuha uses a two-level caching strategy:

  1. CG basis cache (Rust, in-memory + SQLite): Canonical bases are cached inside the Rust layer in a SQLite database. This cache survives between Python sessions.
  2. Symbol cache (Python, SQLite): X-symbol and R-symbol results are cached in separate SQLite databases in the .yuzuha/ directory.

Both caches are thread-safe and transparent — you never need to manage them explicitly. See Database and Cache Management for cache control utilities.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Yuzuha is a Python library with a Rust core, distributed as a binary wheel on PyPI. This guide covers installation options for both end users and contributors.

docs.title: Installing from PyPI
docs.text:
The recommended way to install Yuzuha is via pip:

pip install yuzuha

This installs the pre-compiled Rust extension and the Python package. The only runtime dependency is NumPy 2.0 or higher.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python: 3.11 or higher
  • NumPy: 2.0 or higher

The NumPy floor is not arbitrary: the extension is built against the NumPy 2.x ABI-stable interface, so a 1.x installation will fail at import.

docs.title: Installing from Source
docs.text: If you need the latest development version or want to contribute to Yuzuha, build from source using Maturin.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The crate uses the 2024 edition, so the compiler must be Rust 1.85 or higher. Install Rust and Maturin:

# Install Rust via rustup
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh

# Install Maturin
pip install maturin

docs.title: Building and Installing
docs.text:
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/Ideogenesis-AI/Yuzuha.git
cd Yuzuha

# Build and install in development mode (editable install)
maturin develop --release

# Or install with test dependencies
pip install -e ".[dev]"
maturin develop --release

The --release flag enables Rust optimizations; omit it for faster compile times during development (at the cost of runtime performance).

docs.title: Running Tests
docs.text:
The Python suite runs against whatever build is currently installed in the environment, so run maturin develop first if you have touched the Rust sources:

pytest

The crate also has a Rust-side suite, which needs a feature flag to build; see Contributing for that and for the coverage tooling.

docs.title: Verifying Installation
docs.text:
Verify that Yuzuha is installed and functioning correctly:

import yuzuha

# Create a spin-1/2 representation
j = yuzuha.Spin(1)          # Spin(n) represents j = n/2, so Spin(1) = j=1/2
print(j.value())            # 0.5

# Build a 3rd-order CG specification
spec = yuzuha.CGSpec.from_edges([
    yuzuha.Edge.incoming(j),
    yuzuha.Edge.incoming(j),
    yuzuha.Edge.outgoing(yuzuha.Spin(2)),  # j=1
])
print(spec.num_external())  # 3
print(spec.om_dimension())  # 1

# Compute the canonical basis
import numpy as np
basis = yuzuha.canonical_basis(spec)
print(basis.shape)          # (2, 2, 3, 1)

docs.title: Cache Directory
docs.text:
Yuzuha automatically creates a .yuzuha/ directory in the current working directory to store the SQLite databases for X-symbol, R-symbol, and canonical-basis caches. You can override this location:

# Via environment variable
export YUZUHA_CACHE_PATH=/path/to/cache

# Or programmatically
import yuzuha
yuzuha.set_cache_path('/path/to/cache')

See Cache Management for details.

docs.title: Yuzuha: SU(2) Recoupling Engine
docs.text: Welcome to the documentation for Yuzuha, a high-performance library for computing SU(2) recoupling coefficients in quantum many-body physics and tensor network applications.

docs.title: What is Yuzuha?
docs.text:
Yuzuha provides efficient computation of X-symbols and R-symbols — the fundamental building blocks for contracting and permuting symmetry-constrained tensors in SU(2)-symmetric tensor networks. Created as part of the Ideogenesis-AI effort in studying quantum many-body systems, Yuzuha is optimized as the recoupling engine for the Nicole tensor library while remaining fully usable as a standalone library.

The library is implemented in Rust for performance and exposed to Python via PyO3, providing a zero-copy NumPy interface. Computed canonical CG bases are cached in a local SQLite database, making repeated calculations near-instantaneous.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• X-symbols: Recoupling coefficients for arbitrary tensor network contractions, mapping outer-multiplicity (OM) indices of two input CG tensors to the OM index of their fused output
  • R-symbols: Axis permutation transformations on CG tensors, represented as unitary matrices on the OM space
  • Canonical CG bases: Left-associative fusion-tree bases for arbitrary spin configurations, with systematic OM enumeration
  • CG coefficient engine: Real-valued Condon-Shortley CG coefficients with automatic in-memory caching
  • Invariant metric: Full support for arbitrary arrow directions via the \((-1)^{j-m}\) metric tensor
  • SQLite caching: Persistent, thread-safe database for canonical bases, X-symbols, and R-symbols
  • NumPy integration: Symbols returned as float64 NumPy arrays, compatible with standard scientific Python workflows
  • Rust core: High-performance Rust implementation with a clean Python API

docs.title: Relationship to the Yuzuha Protocol
docs.text: Yuzuha currently implements the SU(2) case of recoupling theory. The interface it provides is designed to generalize to other groups SU(N). The Yuzuha Protocol formally specifies this abstract interface — it defines the types, conventions, and function signatures that any conforming SU(N) recoupling library must satisfy, with the present SU(2) implementation as the reference.

docs.text:
Yuzuha is designed for researchers and developers working on:

  • Tensor Network Algorithms: DMRG, TEBD, PEPS, and other symmetry-aware tensor methods
  • Quantum Many-Body Physics: Systems with SU(2) spin symmetry (e.g. spin-\(\frac{1}{2}\) Heisenberg models, spinful fermion systems like the Hubbard models)
  • Condensed Matter Theory: Frustrated spin systems or strongly correlated spinful fermionic systems with angular momentum conservation
  • Quantum Chemistry: Multi-reference methods with spin-adapted bases

docs.title: Yuzuha Protocol
docs.text: The Yuzuha Protocol is a formal specification for recoupling-coefficient libraries in tensor network applications. It defines the abstract types, self-consistency requirements, and function interfaces that any conforming implementation must satisfy.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Yuzuha currently implements recoupling theory for the SU(2) symmetry group. However, the interface it provides is intentionally designed to generalize to other compact Lie groups, particularly SU(N) for \(N > 2\). The Yuzuha Protocol makes this generalization explicit by separating the abstract interface from the concrete SU(2) implementation.

A library that conforms to the Yuzuha Protocol:

  1. Provides the required abstract types (Type System)
  2. Implements the required symbol functions (Symbol Interface)
  3. Implements the required duality functions (Duality Interface)
  4. Adopts a self-consistent internal convention — the SU(2) Conventions section documents one valid choice used by the reference implementation
  5. Satisfies the caching requirements if caching is implemented (Data Caching)

The current yuzuha Python package is the reference implementation of this protocol for SU(2).

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
The protocol covers:

  • The representation label type — how irreducible representations are identified
  • The edge type — how labeled, directed edges are represented
  • The specification type — how a full fusion tree is described
  • The contraction type — how edge-pair contractions are specified
  • The canonical basis function — normalization and fusion-tree conventions
  • The X-symbol function — its required mathematical properties and API shape
  • The R-symbol function — its required unitarity and composition properties
  • The FS phase function — its required properties and relationship to arrow reversal
  • The conjugate spec function — its required properties and relationship to duality
  • The caching layer — determinism, thread-safety, and key-space requirements

The protocol does not prescribe:

  • Implementation language or performance characteristics
  • Internal algorithms (Racah formula, Wigner 3j/6j, etc.)
  • Specific phase choices, fusion-tree coupling order, or OM-index labeling conventions — any self-consistent choice is valid; the SU(2) Conventions section documents the choices made by the reference implementation
  • The file format of any cache
  • How floating-point precision is handled beyond the requirement that all outputs are real-valued

docs.title: Conformance
docs.text:
A library conforms to the Yuzuha Protocol if:

  1. All required types are present and satisfy the interface constraints in Type System
  2. All outputs satisfy the mathematical identities specified in Symbol Interface and Duality Interface
  3. All error conditions specified in Symbol Interface and Duality Interface are raised with appropriate exceptions
  4. If caching is implemented, it satisfies Data Caching

Conformance may be verified using the protocol's reference test suite (to be published separately).

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text:
The following terms are used throughout this document with their precise meanings:

Term Definition Representation label An element of the set of irreducible representations of the symmetry group Edge A pair (representation label, direction) identifying one external edge of a tensor Spec A complete description of a CG tensor: edges and internal representations Internal representation An intermediate representation appearing in a fusion tree OM dimension Number of valid internal representation paths for a given spec OM index Integer index \(\mu\) labeling one such path Canonical basis The chosen orthonormal basis for the space of CG tensors with a given spec X-symbol Recoupling coefficient tensor for contracting two CG tensors R-symbol Transformation matrix for permuting the edges of a CG tensor

docs.title: Document Structure
docs.text: Page Contents Type System Required types: RepLabel, Direction, Edge, Spec, Contraction Symbol Interface canonical_basis, compute_x_symbol, compute_r_symbol — signatures and properties Duality Interface fs_phase, compute_conjugate — Frobenius-Schur phase and spec dualisation SU(2) Conventions One valid self-consistent convention: phase choices, fusion-tree form, metric Data Caching Key spaces, determinism, thread-safety
